chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Hareez, from Zurara, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

He (peace be upon him) said to me: 'Shall I not point you to something in which the Messenger of God (may God bless him and his family) made no exception?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Supplication repels the decree, even though it has been firmly established.' And he clasped his fingers.

key_terms.أُبرم: Ubrama: made firm, definitively decided, sealed — describing a decree of the highest certainty
key_terms.الدعاء: Du'a: supplication, calling upon God; in Islamic theology a form of worship and a means of changing one's fate
key_terms.القضاء: Al-Qadha: the divine decree, the ordained decision of God regarding a matter; used here as the finalized aspect of divine determination
key_terms.يَسْتَثْنِ: Yastathni: to make an exception or exclusion; the Prophet made no exceptions to the effectiveness of du'a

ai.seo_question: Can supplication (du'a) repel a divine decree in Islam?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) tells Zurara that du'a (supplication) has the power to avert divine decrees even after they have been firmly decreed and established. This hadith affirms that supplication is not futile even when fate appears sealed — the Prophet himself made no exception to this principle. The clasping of fingers by the Imam served as a physical demonstration of the completeness and firmness of the decree that supplication can nonetheless overturn.
